title: How to Criticize and Not Be Hated for It
coreMove: Wrap every correction in one specific, true piece of appreciation, aim the critique at the action rather than the person, and leave them a face-saving way to change.

exampleSpecs.domain: a veteran line cook training a new prep hire during a Friday dinner rush
exampleSpecs.audience: a kitchen lead who has watched two new hires quit after being yelled at
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the new cook stays through the weekend or walks out before the second seating
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the veteran names one true thing she admires about the new cook's knife technique before showing him exactly how she wants the salads plated, and never uses the word 'wrong'

exampleSpecs.domain: a grandfather watching his grandson hold a spinning rod backward on the boy's first real fishing trip
exampleSpecs.audience: a grandparent who remembers being shamed out of a hobby as a child
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the boy ever asks to come fishing again
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the grandfather resists the urge to grab the rod, asks the boy what he is trying to catch, and then offers the grip change as if passing along a small secret rather than a correction

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school band director who publicly dressed down the clarinet section and lost three players the next Monday
exampleSpecs.audience: a teacher rebuilding trust before the spring concert
exampleSpecs.stakes: the concert program and whether the remaining clarinetists ever play with confidence again
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director traces the lost players back to the exact moment of public criticism and rewrites what she should have said one-on-one to a single clarinetist she still respected

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional manager auditing a struggling bakery franchise on two visits a month apart
exampleSpecs.audience: a manager whose blunt feedback has stopped landing with owners
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the owner takes any advice this quarter or starts dodging her calls
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: on the first visit she leads with what is failing and watches the owner's face close; on the second visit she opens with one specific thing she liked about his sourdough display before raising the front-window layout

exampleSpecs.domain: a driving instructor riding shotgun with a 17-year-old who keeps drifting toward the bike lane on a quiet residential street
exampleSpecs.audience: a coach who knows fear destroys learning
exampleSpecs.stakes: the student's confidence and the cyclist three blocks ahead
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: instead of saying 'you're drifting again,' the instructor says 'your hands are quiet, that's good — now feel where your right tire is right now,' so the student notices the error himself

exampleSpecs.domain: a senior surgeon supervising a resident whose suturing tension is loose mid-procedure
exampleSpecs.audience: a surgical preceptor who was once humiliated in a teaching hospital
exampleSpecs.stakes: the patient on the table and the resident's willingness to ask for help next time
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the surgeon praises the resident's knot placement honestly, then asks for 'a half-millimeter more bite on the next throw,' framing the fix as the next move rather than a verdict on the last one
